claim: Adults taking over-the-counter ibuprofen should not exceed 1,200 mg in 24 hours unless directed by a healthcare professional.
label: not_found
evidence: Label says ‘do not exceed 6 tablets in 24 hours’ but never states mg

claim: Adults can typically take 200–400 mg of ibuprofen every 4–6 hours as needed, following the product label.
label: not_found
evidence: Label says ‘1 tablet every 4 to 6 hours’ but gives no mg amount

claim: Ibuprofen should be taken with food or milk to help reduce stomach irritation.
label: supported
evidence: take with food or milk if stomach upset occurs

claim: Ibuprofen can cause stomach ulcers and serious gastrointestinal bleeding, even without warning symptoms.
label: supported

claim: Ibuprofen can increase the risk of heart attack and stroke, particularly with higher doses or prolonged use.
label: supported
evidence: NSAIDs increase the risk of heart attack, heart failure, and stroke; higher if you use more than directed or for longer than directed

claim: Ibuprofen can cause kidney damage, especially in people with existing kidney disease or dehydration.
label: not_found
evidence: Only says to ask a doctor if you have kidney disease; nothing about kidney damage

claim: Ibuprofen can interfere with the heart-protective antiplatelet effect of low-dose aspirin when taken at certain times.
label: supported
evidence: ibuprofen may decrease this benefit of aspirin

claim: Combining ibuprofen with blood thinners such as warfarin can increase the risk of serious bleeding.
label: supported
evidence: Bleeding chance is higher if you take a blood thinning (anticoagulant) drug

claim: Ibuprofen should generally be avoided from 20 weeks of pregnancy unless specifically advised by a healthcare professional, and avoided at 30 weeks or later.
label: supported
evidence: especially important not to use ibuprofen at 20 weeks or later in pregnancy

claim: Ibuprofen dosing for children is based on the child’s weight and age, and adult doses should not be given to children.
label: not_found
evidence: Only says children under 12 years: ask a doctor; nothing about weight-based dosing
